- [CADT-IDRI/khmer-multifont-ocr](https://huggingface.co/datasets/CADT-IDRI/khmer-multifont-ocr) — text-recognition: 
	
		
	
	
		Khmer Multi-Font OCR
	

393 images of clean rendered Khmer text in ten Khmer OS fonts. The same source
text is rendered in every font, so content and total text length are identical
across fonts and only the typeface (and the resulting page layout) varies. The
number of images per font differs (34-48) because glyph width and letter design
change how much text fits on each image.

Used in: Distilling Multimodal Foundation Models into Lightweight OCR for
Low-Resource Khmer (ACET).… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/CADT-IDRI/khmer-multifont-ocr.

## Paper

- [Reading Between the Layers: Cross-Modal Alignment and Representational Hierarchy in Vision Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32463) — text-recognition: While large vision-language models excel at optical character recognition, it remains unclear how their underlying vision encoders process text and its meaning, and whether they support anything resembling reading comprehension. We systematically study transformer-based vision encoders, using cross-modal alignment between rendered text and visual concepts together with probing and retrieval-based analyses as a controlled window into these broader capabilities. Our layer-wise analyses span orthographic, grammatical, and semantic organization, and reveal that strong cross-modal mapping emerges only in the deepest layers, after unimodal object and text recognition have already developed, coinciding with a progression from surface-level to semantic representations. Although this hierarchy is strongest in contrastively trained models, larger self-supervised models and text-rich training data partially support similar behaviors without explicit language supervision. Together, our results suggest that increasing model and training-data scale, as well as text-rich training data, can partially compensate for the absence of language supervision.
